Cerebras, a maker of artificial intelligence chips, has been on file since late September, and online lender Klarna said last week that it has confidentially filed its IPO paperwork with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission.

Steckelberg announced her departure from Zoom in August after seven years at the company. Last month, former Microsoft executive Michelle Chang replaced Steckelberg as Zoom's CFO.

Operator Spotlight
Finance & Legal
Meet Canva CFO Kelly Steckelberg

By
Caroline Caswell
“How did they do that? How did they get there?” Companies succeed because of the people who build them - operating leaders who grow businesses to new heights and make decisions every day that can impact entire industries. Our Operator Spotlight gives you the inside track from one of our incredible Operator LPs (Limited Partners) who are changing the game – building and scaling some of the world’s most successful companies. Read on for lessons learned and mistakes made, perspectives from the top, practical advice, and ideas on what’s next.
‍
This month, we chatted with Kelly Steckelberg, the Chief Financial Officer at Canva. Kelly leads the global finance organization, supporting the company’s mission to empower the world to design. Since its launch in 2013, Canva has become one of the world’s most valuable private companies, generating over $2.7 billion in annualised revenue and serving more than 230 million users across the globe. Prior to joining Canva, Kelly served as CFO at Zoom, where she helped guide the company through its initial public offering and a subsequent period of hypergrowth stemming from the pandemic. She has also held leadership roles as CFO and CEO of Zoosk and divisional CFO for the Consumer Segment and WebEx at Cisco. Kelly began her career at KPMG, working in both tax and audit.
‍
You've been the CFO through some of the most defining moments in tech - from Zoom's IPO and pandemic hypergrowth to now scaling Canva past $2.5B in revenue. What's the biggest difference in how you approach the CFO role between a public company experiencing sudden explosive growth versus a high-growth private company like Canva?
There are actually a lot of similarities between these two companies in terms of having an amazing product that is very viral in nature, with tremendous customer love and a focus on solving customer problems. The difference between being public and private is that you have more flexibility while you're still private and before you step onto the public stage. We did this at Zoom too - really focusing on investing to ensure we have long-term sustainable growth before going public. At Canva, we aspire to be a generational company, so building that foundation as a private company is really critical. While there are differences between public vs. private, ultimately, it’s always about creating long term impact, not just short term momentum.
‍
You've built and scaled finance organizations at some of the fastest-growing tech companies of the last decade. How are you thinking about retooling the office of the CFO with AI? What specific processes or functions have you found most ripe for AI transformation, and where do you still see the need for human judgment and oversight?
The way we're thinking about AI is that it absolutely augments everything we do and drives efficiency. Depending on the process, maybe it gets us 40% there, maybe 70%, and then humans finish it. But I think the big difference from 10 years ago and honestly, even eight months ago when I started, is what the future of systems and that roadmap looks like. For example, I'm not sure that everything sits within a massive ERP system any longer. There are opportunities for AI to radically change some of those processes. So before we start investing, we're really thinking thoughtfully about what this is going to look like two or three years from now. We also look to trusted advisors and leaders in the space to help us expand our vantage point on what's possible.
‍
At Canva, we’re part of the AI-native generation of companies. If AI is in our product, it has to be embedded in our operations too. We’ve succeeded through a mix of building and buying. Long before the recent AI wave, we were already an AI-enabled platform, leading with that mindset.
‍  
While quite a bit has been built in-house, we’ve also made game changing acquisitions, from Kaleido way back in 2021 to Leonardo.ai and Magic Brief in the last year - all design-led companies to power our long term efforts. What’s worked especially well are small to mid-sized acquisitions that combine strategic tech tuck-ins with attracting exceptional talent.  For us, this is ultimately both fueling product innovation and significant R&D.
‍
How have you seen the CFO role evolve over the last decade? What skills or focus areas that weren't critical 10 years ago are now essential for finance leaders?
What’s changed dramatically is that it’s just not enough to only understand and talk about the financials. You have to be a strong storyteller; someone who can weave the numbers into a compelling narrative about the business, the product, the strategy and explain why it all matters. Investors want to dig a lot deeper in all of those other areas, so it goes so far beyond just the numbers. You have to connect the dots, bringing the overall strategy to life, and show that you're an expert in all aspects of the business, not just the balance sheet.
‍
Having lived through Zoom's pandemic moment, you've seen firsthand how external forces can create unprecedented growth. How do you build processes that can scale both up and down rapidly when the unexpected happens?
It comes down to having the right foundation. At both Canva and previously at Zoom, we’re really thoughtful about where we want to invest for long-term, sustainable growth and making sure that is the priority. At both companies, that has meant focusing on areas of product, engineering, and sales capacity because those are really the long term sustainable drivers. And then being very, very thoughtful and frugal about G&A and any aspects of the cost of goods sold. How can you automate or bring in third party vendors to help you flex up and potentially down as needed? That's what we did during the pandemic. Certain areas that we thought would get more automated over time - for example, customer success - we brought in third party vendors to help us scale up and then we were able to scale down as needed.
‍
Especially when you come in early, there can be a mindset (and often external validation) that top line growth hides all sins. As long as you're growing, you can just spend and do whatever you want! But that is not sustainable. The best way to adjust is to be prepared ideally before, but even while you’re in growth mode. Before something happens, you need to have that discipline and help teams prioritize. Instead of having "and" conversations you start having "or" conversations, which can help people realize that unfettered spending does not live forever. The earlier you can start to influence that mindset, the better off you are.
‍
You've traveled to over 70 countries! How has that global perspective influenced your approach to scaling international operations for companies that serve a truly global user base?
I actually lived in Amsterdam for three and a half years as a European Finance Director at PeopleSoft. That really kicked off the realization of how differently business works around the world. How you have to really be thoughtful about how things translate.
‍  
And kind of a joke, but kind of a reality too; this was pretty eye opening to me when I moved from California back to Texas two years ago. It’s healthy to get outside of whatever bubble you might be closest to, and I think it’s very important for leaders to have different perspectives across management, policies, and products.
‍
At Canva, the vast majority  of our employees, including our founders and most of our leaders, are in Sydney.  We also have teams spread out across 10 offices, so a  truly global operation. That means thinking about where you need what kind of talent. With roots that didn’t start in Silicon Valley, it's never been a given that everybody's going to be in the Bay Area, or the US for that matter.   
And how do I support our business partners in such radically different time zones or different cultures? Well, it’s proven to be an amazing opportunity to be intentional  and ensure that we really have a global-first team mentality, building inclusively across every single time zone.
‍
As someone who's been on the buying side of enterprise software, what advice would you offer early-stage founders building products for CFOs and finance teams? What are the biggest mistakes you see founders make when trying to crack into enterprise finance organizations, and what immediately signals to you that a vendor "gets it"?
I think the biggest mistake is assuming they know what their prospects' problems are. It may or may not be something that you're focused on at all, and that’s really the key. So the flip side where I’ve seen it be more effective is if you can understand what they're actually focused on. Also, it might not be the right time for you, but you can build a relationship over time.   
I’m actually living that reality right now  - I'm thinking about a systems roadmap. I have met some founders of companies, and am learning a lot, but I am not ready to make a decision right now. But that doesn't mean a year from now I won't come back to them! So my advice would be to think of it as a process. It might be a long process, and it's a relationship builder at first, but has the potential to work on both sides.
‍
What's your secret super power?
I've been doing this for a long time! I’m able to assess quickly and see around corners because I have seen a lot of these situations before - both for opportunities and potential pitfalls that we might face.
‍
What's a piece of advice you would give to yourself 10 years ago, if you had the opportunity?
Stop stressing and enjoy it more. I love my job, and I’ve loved it for a long time - but I would say only in the last six or seven years have I let myself really appreciate how amazing it is, and not be completely stressed all the time. I'm not going to say it's not stressful, but I don’t let it overtake my life.

Canva Pty Ltd is an Australian multinational software company launched in 2013. The platform provides a graphic design platform to create visual content for presentations, websites, and other digital products. Its uses include templates for presentations, posters, and social media content, as well as photo and video editing functionality.
The platform uses a drag-and-drop interface designed for its users without professional design training or experience. Canva operates on a freemium model and has added features such as print services and video editing tools over time.
History
[edit]
2013–2020
[edit]
Canva was founded in Perth, Australia, by Melanie Perkins, Cliff Obrecht and Cameron Adams on 1 January 2013. One of the company's early investors was Susan Wu "Susan Wu (entrepreneur)"), an American entrepreneur. In its first year, Canva had more than 750,000 users. In 2017, the company reached profitability and had 294,000 paying customers.
In January 2018, Perkins announced that the company had raised A$40 million from Sequoia Capital, Blackbird Ventures, and Felicis Ventures, and was valued at A$1 billion. It raised A$70 million in May 2019 and A$85 million in October 2019, when Canva for Enterprise launched.
In December 2019, Canva announced Canva for Education, a free product for educational institutions intended to facilitate collaboration between students and teachers.
In 2020, Canva announced a partnership with FedEx Office in June and with Office Depot in July.
2021–2025
[edit]
In September 2021, Canva raised US$200 million, with its value peaking that year at US$40 billion. By September 2022, its valuation had levelled at US$26 billion.
While Canva's value declined from its 2021 peak by mid-2022, it remained one of Australia's most prominent technology companies, alongside Atlassian. In 2023, the pair were named in the Australian Financial Review's AFR Rich List as among the 10 most wealthy people in Australia.
On 7 December 2022, Canva launched Magic Write, the platform's AI-powered copywriting assistant. On 22 March 2023, it announced its Assistant tool, which makes recommendations on graphics and styles that match the user's existing design. On 11 January 2024, Canva launched its own GPT in OpenAI's GPT Store.
In May 2024, the company announced the launch of Canva Enterprise, a plan designed for large organisations, alongside tools including Work Kits, Courses and AI capabilities. In 2024, it announced a co-funded solar energy project to enhance its sustainability efforts.
In February 2025, Canva reorganised its corporate group. A newly incorporated Delaware company, Canva, Inc., became the group's ultimate holding company. The former parent was subsequently registered in Australia as Canva Australia Holdings Pty Ltd, while the group's business operations were intended to continue in substantially the same manner.
On 10 April 2025, Canva released Visual Suite 2. The interface combines Canva's design and productivity tools. Features include a spreadsheets application (Canva Sheets), a generative AI coding assistant (Canva Code), a chatbot, and an updated photo editor that can modify or remove background objects.
In August 2025, Canva launched a stock sale to employees, valuing the company at US$42 billion.
In October 2025, Canva introduced a design model capable of generating layouts with separately editable layers and objects. It also relaunched Affinity as a unified application combining vector, pixel and page-layout tools and made the base application free to use.
By the end of 2025, Canva reported more than 265 million monthly active users and more than 31 million paid users. Its annual recurring revenue reached US$4 billion, including US$500 million from business customers with more than 25 seats.
2026-present
[edit]
In April 2026, Canva introduced Canva AI 2.0 in research preview, adding agentic tools that can schedule and perform recurring design tasks in the background. The company also added an offline mode that allows selected designs to be edited without an internet connection and synchronised when connectivity returns.
In August 2026, Canva reduced its expected annual revenue-growth rate from 30% to 20%. The company said unexpectedly high costs associated with serving its AI features had led it to slow their rollout while rebuilding the underlying architecture. Chief executive Melanie Perkins said that the cost per AI task had fallen by nearly 90% since Canva AI 2.0 was introduced in April.
Acquisitions
[edit]
In 2018, Canva acquired presentations startup Zeetings for an undisclosed amount, as part of its expansion into the presentations space.
In May 2019, Canva announced the acquisitions of Pixabay and Pexels, two free stock photography sites based in Germany, which enabled Canva users to access their photos for designs.
In February 2021, Canva acquired Austrian startup Kaleido.ai and the Czech-based Smartmockups.
In 2022, Canva acquired Flourish, a London-based data visualization startup.
In March 2024, Canva acquired UK-based Serif, the developers of the Affinity suite of graphic design software, for approximately $380 million.
In August 2024, Canva acquired the AI image generation platform and startup, Leonardo AI, for an undisclosed amount.
In June 2025, it was announced that Canva had acquired Australian AI marketing startup MagicBrief for an undisclosed amount.
In February 2026, Canva acquired two startups: Cavalry, which specializes in animation software, and MangoAI, which aims to optimize advertising performance.
In April 2026, Canva acquired Simtheory, an AI Workflow Tool, and Ortto, a marketing automation tool.
Philanthropy
[edit]
Canva's co-founders, Melanie Perkins and Cliff Obrecht, have said they intend to donate a significant part of their personal wealth to charity.
In 2021, Canva started a partnership with GiveDirectly, a nonprofit organization operating in low-income areas that makes unconditional cash transfers to families living in extreme poverty. Since then, the company has donated $50 million to support GiveDirectly's work across Malawi.
In 2025, Canva announced an additional $100 million commitment to expand its GiveDirectly partnership.
2019 data breach
[edit]
A May 2019 data breach exposed roughly 139 million Canva users' data. The exposed data included real names of users, usernames, email addresses, geographical information, and password hashes.
In January 2020, about 4 million Canva user passwords were decrypted and shared online. Canva responded by resetting the passwords of every user who had not changed their password since the initial breach.

CFO of the Year: Kelly Steckelberg, Zoom
The veteran CFO has used strategic insight and operational experience to help one of the biggest beneficiaries of the pandemic manage its meteoric growth.
Zoom
Courtesy of Zoom
When Zoom CEO Eric Yuan hired Kelly Steckelberg to be his company’s first CFO in 2017, he had his sights set on going public and needed an experienced hand to help him prepare for and manage the IPO. He got that. But he also got a former CEO whose experience on the strategic side of running a company made her the ideal partner to manage Zoom’s explosive pandemic-led growth.
“We didn’t hire Kelly because we are going to go public,” Yuan told the Silicon Valley Business Journal at the time. “It’s more to help us grow our business.”
Yuan and Steckelberg worked together at WebEx, the video conferencing platform Cisco bought in 2007. For all of WebEx’s promise, Yuan said, it was too hard for people to use. That led him and other engineers to leave and build from scratch what they hoped would be a reliable, user-friendly platform: Zoom.

Kelly Steckelberg
Courtesy of Zoom
Steckelberg, who was finance chief and then CEO of dating app Zoosk after she left WebEx, was the natural choice to join her former colleagues.
“Having the opportunity to be CFO at Zoom was something I just couldn’t pass up,” she said.
For her role managing a company that, because of the pandemic, grew 355% over two quarters and became a household name, Steckelberg is CFO Dive’s CFO of the Year.
“Kelly and her team have done a tremendous job,” says Ryan Koontz, who follows Zoom as managing director of Rosenblatt Securities. “She’s an integral part of the machine there.”
Empowering success
Steckelberg brings two guiding principles to her role as CFO: Employees should think of the company’s finances as their own, and they should understand how their role contributes to the company’s success.
“If you give employees the opportunity to understand how they fit in, most will rise to the occasion and do everything they can to help,” she said. “Everybody wants to participate in the company’s financial success.”
Steckelberg credits her three years as CEO of Zoosk with giving her organization-wide insight.
“It gave me a much greater understanding of how marketing, engineering, and product development come together,” she said. “If we’re launching a product, what does that mean for needs that ripple across the whole organization? I’m more able to prompt people to think, if we’re adding all this headcount over here, don’t we need something on this side as well?”
Zoosk was a popular dating app when Steckelberg joined it as finance chief in 2011, but it ran into trouble while preparing for an IPO in 2014. Its losses were mounting despite having 27 million users and $200 million in revenue.
With critics saying the company was focusing too much on growth at the expense of profitability, the company canceled its IPO and Steckelberg was promoted to CEO. The job forced her to make tough calls, including laying off 15% of the staff and reducing marketing spend.
“Reductions in force are the hardest decisions you have to make,” she said.
A key to the company’s turnaround was her executive team’s decision to change the direction of the product and eliminate features that would decrease its revenue in the short term.
“That was a very difficult decision to make,” she said. “It’s absolutely counter-intuitive to everything you learn as a finance person. But two years later, our strategy really took hold.”
Managing growth
Zoom was already a high-flying company when she left Zoosk in 2017, but the pandemic supercharged its growth in a way few businesses have experienced.
“It just happened to be they were at the right place at the right time,” Koontz said. “They literally accelerated about four years’ worth of growth into two quarters. And there aren’t too many types of products or services you can sell in the world that can actually produce that. Zoom is a verb now.”
Koontz credits Steckelberg and her team with managing the company’s meteoric rise with the right mix of short- and long-term investment while executing an aggressive organization-wide hiring plan. The company has grown from about 700 employees to 4,000 in the last three years, and needs more, but the pandemic has slowed hiring.
“I know they paid out bonuses to a lot of employees over the third quarter, during the pandemic, just for the workload these people had to incur because they literally couldn’t hire fast enough,” Koontz said.
He praised the company’s decision to open its two newest R&D centers in Arizona and Pennsylvania rather than in Silicon Valley or other technology hubs. “These are places where you can hire engineers,” he said.
The company’s decision to add server capacity by partnering with Oracle, rather than building additional in-house data centers, is another smart move, because it provides the kind of flexibility that it can turn on and off as needed in the short-term.
“Their margins took a little bit of a hit because they had to use public cloud instead of building their own infrastructure out in some places,” he said. “You can basically order up the level of service you need on an hour-to-hour basis to handle your peak loads, so they’re basically using public cloud to handle the peaks and to handle the surges in demand where they just aren’t ready with their own infrastructure.”
“It gives us the ability to flex up and down as we need to going forward,” Steckelberg said. “We’re being thoughtful about not getting over-committed from a resource perspective and looking where we can use third-party resources to flex. We’re going to have this hybrid approach.”
The mix worked well when usage dropped over the summer when online classes concluded and then picked up again in the fall.
To know whether more server capacity is needed, Steckelberg said, she looks at a metric she didn’t pay much attention to before the pandemic: concurrent daily meeting attendees. Previously, she looked at daily meeting attendees as a gauge of company performance. But now, she needs to know how many people are video conferencing at the same time.
“It’s become more important over the last six months,” she said. “It tells us where we’re going and what we need to add.”
Long-term plan
The company’s biggest challenge lies ahead: staying on a growth trajectory once the pandemic eases and the demand for video conferencing subsides.
After Pfizer in early November announced a 90% success rate with its vaccine in tests, Zoom’s stock valuation dropped 17%, a preview of what’s to come if it can’t show a renewed growth path.
But the company’s strategy so far has been reassuring, Koontz said. In one of its biggest moves, it launched Zoom Phone, a kind of PBX system in which calls, whether for work, home or mobile, are routed through a single system and can be converted to a video call. RingCentral is a dominant player in the space, but it might not be for long.
“Maybe Zoom wants to be the king of unified communications and buy RingCentral,” he said.
The company has already snapped up RingCentral’s former chief sales executive, Ryan Azus, another WebEx alum, suggesting it is keeping a close eye on the company.
Zoom has also been making its core video conferencing business more attractive for a post-pandemic world. Companies have seen how cost- and time-efficient video conferencing can be compared to on-site events, which makes them likely to make virtual events a bigger part of how they operate even while resuming travel.
Zoom’s improvements include a partnership with DocuSign to enable contract signings during virtual meetings and the launch of a program called OnZoom, which is intended to increase the attraction of virtual meetings for small businesses. Other initiatives include voiceless check-ins and what Zoom calls its Smart Gallery, a way for employees attending an in-person meeting virtually to feel more a part of the event.
“We’re always listening to our customers and learning from them what is the most beneficial to them,” Steckelberg said. “As long as we keep focused on that, competition makes us all be better. It’s good for the end user.”
“I think they’re doing the best they can given the circumstances,” Koontz said. “Their op ex in the July quarter was up 104% YOY, so they doubled in size in a single year, and they’re still behind. It’s pretty incredible what they’re trying to pull off.”

Canva, a high-valued design software startup that competes with Adobe, said Monday that it hired Kelly Steckelberg as its chief financial officer, five years after she helped take Zoom public and then guided the company through its Covid-19 pandemic surge.
Founded in 2013, Canva was valued recently at $32 billion, a drop from its peak of $40 billion in 2021.
"Kelly's impressive track record as a strong leader and strategic thinker, combined with her proven expertise in scaling enterprise companies, make her the perfect addition to our leadership bench," Canva said in an emailed statement.
Canva is generating about $2.5 billion in annualized revenue and boasts 220 million monthly users. The company is widely viewed as a top initial public offering candidate for venture-backed tech companies after a historically slow period for new offerings dating back to early 2022.
On Monday, ServiceTitan, which sells software for the trades, filed to list on the Nasdaq. Cerebras, a maker of artificial intelligence chips, has been on file since late September, and online lender Klarna said last week that it has confidentially filed its IPO paperwork with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission.
A Canva spokesperson declined to comment on the startup's timeline for an IPO.
Steckelberg held financial positions at Cisco and was CEO of online dating company Zoosk before joining Zoom in 2017. Steckelberg is based in Austin, Texas, while Canva has its headquarters in Sydney, Australia.
Zoom went public with Steckelberg's help in 2019. The video-chat company saw its market cap soar to upward of $160 billion in October 2020, early in the Covid-19 pandemic, as users working from home swarmed to the app. Zoom has since lost more than 85% of its value.
Steckelberg announced her departure from Zoom in August after seven years at the company. Last month, former Microsoft executive Michelle Chang replaced Steckelberg as Zoom's CFO.
Canva's previous finance chief Damien Singh resigned in February after the company said it was conducting an internal investigation surrounding inappropriate behavior.

Operator Spotlight
Finance & Legal
Meet Canva CFO Kelly Steckelberg

By
Caroline Caswell
“How did they do that? How did they get there?” Companies succeed because of the people who build them - operating leaders who grow businesses to new heights and make decisions every day that can impact entire industries. Our Operator Spotlight gives you the inside track from one of our incredible Operator LPs (Limited Partners) who are changing the game – building and scaling some of the world’s most successful companies. Read on for lessons learned and mistakes made, perspectives from the top, practical advice, and ideas on what’s next.
‍
This month, we chatted with Kelly Steckelberg, the Chief Financial Officer at Canva. Kelly leads the global finance organization, supporting the company’s mission to empower the world to design. Since its launch in 2013, Canva has become one of the world’s most valuable private companies, generating over $2.7 billion in annualised revenue and serving more than 230 million users across the globe. Prior to joining Canva, Kelly served as CFO at Zoom, where she helped guide the company through its initial public offering and a subsequent period of hypergrowth stemming from the pandemic. She has also held leadership roles as CFO and CEO of Zoosk and divisional CFO for the Consumer Segment and WebEx at Cisco. Kelly began her career at KPMG, working in both tax and audit.
‍
You've been the CFO through some of the most defining moments in tech - from Zoom's IPO and pandemic hypergrowth to now scaling Canva past $2.5B in revenue. What's the biggest difference in how you approach the CFO role between a public company experiencing sudden explosive growth versus a high-growth private company like Canva?
There are actually a lot of similarities between these two companies in terms of having an amazing product that is very viral in nature, with tremendous customer love and a focus on solving customer problems. The difference between being public and private is that you have more flexibility while you're still private and before you step onto the public stage. We did this at Zoom too - really focusing on investing to ensure we have long-term sustainable growth before going public. At Canva, we aspire to be a generational company, so building that foundation as a private company is really critical. While there are differences between public vs. private, ultimately, it’s always about creating long term impact, not just short term momentum.
‍
You've built and scaled finance organizations at some of the fastest-growing tech companies of the last decade. How are you thinking about retooling the office of the CFO with AI? What specific processes or functions have you found most ripe for AI transformation, and where do you still see the need for human judgment and oversight?
The way we're thinking about AI is that it absolutely augments everything we do and drives efficiency. Depending on the process, maybe it gets us 40% there, maybe 70%, and then humans finish it. But I think the big difference from 10 years ago and honestly, even eight months ago when I started, is what the future of systems and that roadmap looks like. For example, I'm not sure that everything sits within a massive ERP system any longer. There are opportunities for AI to radically change some of those processes. So before we start investing, we're really thinking thoughtfully about what this is going to look like two or three years from now. We also look to trusted advisors and leaders in the space to help us expand our vantage point on what's possible.
‍
At Canva, we’re part of the AI-native generation of companies. If AI is in our product, it has to be embedded in our operations too. We’ve succeeded through a mix of building and buying. Long before the recent AI wave, we were already an AI-enabled platform, leading with that mindset.
‍  
While quite a bit has been built in-house, we’ve also made game changing acquisitions, from Kaleido way back in 2021 to Leonardo.ai and Magic Brief in the last year - all design-led companies to power our long term efforts. What’s worked especially well are small to mid-sized acquisitions that combine strategic tech tuck-ins with attracting exceptional talent.  For us, this is ultimately both fueling product innovation and significant R&D.
‍
How have you seen the CFO role evolve over the last decade? What skills or focus areas that weren't critical 10 years ago are now essential for finance leaders?
What’s changed dramatically is that it’s just not enough to only understand and talk about the financials. You have to be a strong storyteller; someone who can weave the numbers into a compelling narrative about the business, the product, the strategy and explain why it all matters. Investors want to dig a lot deeper in all of those other areas, so it goes so far beyond just the numbers. You have to connect the dots, bringing the overall strategy to life, and show that you're an expert in all aspects of the business, not just the balance sheet.
‍
Having lived through Zoom's pandemic moment, you've seen firsthand how external forces can create unprecedented growth. How do you build processes that can scale both up and down rapidly when the unexpected happens?
It comes down to having the right foundation. At both Canva and previously at Zoom, we’re really thoughtful about where we want to invest for long-term, sustainable growth and making sure that is the priority. At both companies, that has meant focusing on areas of product, engineering, and sales capacity because those are really the long term sustainable drivers. And then being very, very thoughtful and frugal about G&A and any aspects of the cost of goods sold. How can you automate or bring in third party vendors to help you flex up and potentially down as needed? That's what we did during the pandemic. Certain areas that we thought would get more automated over time - for example, customer success - we brought in third party vendors to help us scale up and then we were able to scale down as needed.
‍
Especially when you come in early, there can be a mindset (and often external validation) that top line growth hides all sins. As long as you're growing, you can just spend and do whatever you want! But that is not sustainable. The best way to adjust is to be prepared ideally before, but even while you’re in growth mode. Before something happens, you need to have that discipline and help teams prioritize. Instead of having "and" conversations you start having "or" conversations, which can help people realize that unfettered spending does not live forever. The earlier you can start to influence that mindset, the better off you are.
‍
You've traveled to over 70 countries! How has that global perspective influenced your approach to scaling international operations for companies that serve a truly global user base?
I actually lived in Amsterdam for three and a half years as a European Finance Director at PeopleSoft. That really kicked off the realization of how differently business works around the world. How you have to really be thoughtful about how things translate.
‍  
And kind of a joke, but kind of a reality too; this was pretty eye opening to me when I moved from California back to Texas two years ago. It’s healthy to get outside of whatever bubble you might be closest to, and I think it’s very important for leaders to have different perspectives across management, policies, and products.
‍
At Canva, the vast majority  of our employees, including our founders and most of our leaders, are in Sydney.  We also have teams spread out across 10 offices, so a  truly global operation. That means thinking about where you need what kind of talent. With roots that didn’t start in Silicon Valley, it's never been a given that everybody's going to be in the Bay Area, or the US for that matter.   
And how do I support our business partners in such radically different time zones or different cultures? Well, it’s proven to be an amazing opportunity to be intentional  and ensure that we really have a global-first team mentality, building inclusively across every single time zone.
‍
As someone who's been on the buying side of enterprise software, what advice would you offer early-stage founders building products for CFOs and finance teams? What are the biggest mistakes you see founders make when trying to crack into enterprise finance organizations, and what immediately signals to you that a vendor "gets it"?
I think the biggest mistake is assuming they know what their prospects' problems are. It may or may not be something that you're focused on at all, and that’s really the key. So the flip side where I’ve seen it be more effective is if you can understand what they're actually focused on. Also, it might not be the right time for you, but you can build a relationship over time.   
I’m actually living that reality right now  - I'm thinking about a systems roadmap. I have met some founders of companies, and am learning a lot, but I am not ready to make a decision right now. But that doesn't mean a year from now I won't come back to them! So my advice would be to think of it as a process. It might be a long process, and it's a relationship builder at first, but has the potential to work on both sides.
‍
What's your secret super power?
I've been doing this for a long time! I’m able to assess quickly and see around corners because I have seen a lot of these situations before - both for opportunities and potential pitfalls that we might face.
‍
What's a piece of advice you would give to yourself 10 years ago, if you had the opportunity?
Stop stressing and enjoy it more. I love my job, and I’ve loved it for a long time - but I would say only in the last six or seven years have I let myself really appreciate how amazing it is, and not be completely stressed all the time. I'm not going to say it's not stressful, but I don’t let it overtake my life.

Canva announces major job cuts after 'our hardest year yet'

Getty A woman with long dark hair wearing a black jacket gestures with her hands
Canva, one of Australia's best known start-ups, has announced a shake up of the business that will affect 22% of its workers, including job cuts.
In what was "without doubt the hardest moment in our thirteen-year history" co-founder and CEO Melanie Perkins said 1,271 people would either lose their jobs, be asked to relocate or change roles.
The firm's value has reportedly dropped in the past year over concerns about the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) on its business as well as the cost of incorporating the technology into its platforms.
It had been "our hardest year yet, and as we shared earlier this year, our growth has slowed for the first time in a decade," Perkins wrote to staff.
The "incredibly hard decision" meant "significant changes," Perkins said.
"For some people, this will mean changes to their roles or being asked to relocate to centralised hubs. Sadly, it will also mean saying goodbye to teammates and friends who have helped build Canva into what it is today."
The company, which has staff in 37 countries, said Sydney would become the "primary home" for more of its product teams and that as of next year hybrid workers would be expected to spend two to three days in the office.
Earlier this year two of its backers, Blackbird Ventures and Airtree, reportedly downgraded its valuation from A$60bn ($41.8bn; £31.1bn) at the end of last year to about A$49bn.
Canva also reportedly cut its own internal valuation amid soaring AI expenses related to the roll out of new products.
"New technology is transforming what people can create, how they create it, and what they expect from the products they use," Perkins said in her note on Wednesday.
Perkins, who left university at 19 to found her first venture, launched Canva in 2013.

Canva appears to have accelerated the build-out of its US public-company infrastructure, hiring senior staff to rehearse earnings calls, manage sell-side analysts, prepare financial guidance and strengthen the financial systems needed to operate under public-market scrutiny.
Canva has been open for years about its intention to ultimately list, but the company has recently been hit by turbulence with its valuation cut amid concerns about competition from frontier AI models.
However the latest hiring indicates the company is strengthening the team and processes required to run a US public company.
At Canva Create in April, co-founder Cliff Obrecht told Capital Brief the company was “fully IPO ready” and said he assumed it would list in 2027, but stressed Canva wanted to bed down its shift to an AI-credit business model before exposing that transition to public-market scrutiny.
Since then, uncertainty around the timing has grown amid the increasing cost of its AI overhaul and delays to key products.
A Canva spokesperson told Capital Brief there was nothing new to share regarding an IPO.

What’s New: Our latest launches you won’t want to miss
What’s New: Our latest launches you won’t want to miss
This month's launches are all about closing the gap between creating and sharing, with sharper AI, smoother workflows, and more ways to publish directly from Canva.
At Canva, we know designing something is only half the story. The other half is everything that comes after: getting it looking right, getting it out into the world, and making sure it lands the way you intended. That's what this month is really about.
We're rolling out sharper AI tools, a growing suite of publishing integrations that connect Canva to the platforms you already rely on, and a collection of workflow improvements that came directly from conversations with our community. Some of these updates are big, some are small, but all of them are designed to make the journey from idea to impact feel a little more like flow and a little less like effort.
Here's what's new.
Supercharge your creativity with Canva AI
Remove anything from a photo, cleaner than ever
Magic Eraser⁠(opens in a new tab or window) has always made it simple to remove unwanted objects from your photos – and now, the results are even better. We've improved the quality under the hood so removals are cleaner and more natural-looking, with no shadows or reflections left behind. Whether you're tidying up a product shot or removing a photobomber from an otherwise perfect travel snap, just brush or click what you want gone and Canva takes care of the rest.
Bring your photos to life, now with faces
Image to Video⁠(opens in a new tab or window) has been a favorite since we launched it, and this month it’s had an upgrade! Quality and performance are both improved, and for the first time, Image to Video now supports human faces, so portraits and photos featuring people animate naturally and realistically. Turn a still shot into five seconds of polished video content with a single click, no filming or editing required.
Design faster and smarter
See your website on mobile as you build it
When you're designing a website, knowing how it'll look on a phone shouldn't require publishing it first. Live Previews lets you toggle to a mobile view directly in the Canva Website editor, so layout, spacing, and visual changes update in real time as you work. It takes the guesswork out of mobile design and means you can refine with confidence before anything goes live.
Keep your brand colours working together
Having the right colours in your Brand Kit⁠(opens in a new tab or window) is only half the job, and knowing how to combine them is the other. Colour themes lets brand admins define exactly how colours work together across backgrounds, elements, and text, then apply that combination to any design in a single click. Team members can shuffle between themes to explore different looks, with the confidence that every option stays on-brand, closing one of the more persistent gaps in brand governance for teams designing at scale.
More control over your presenter notes
Preparing a presentation⁠(opens in a new tab or window) now comes with a few welcome additions to the Notes panel. You can generate notes using a custom prompt, see estimated speaker time per page and for the full presentation, and adjust font size directly in the panel — so you can walk into any room with notes that suit your presenting style.
Small changes, real time saved
Some of the most-requested improvements are also the quietest. All three of these have been long-standing requests from our community:
🎨 You can now change all colours or fonts on a single page in one go, without touching the rest of your design.

🗂️ Grouped elements now nest as a layer group in the Position Panel, making it easier to read your design's structure at a glance and adjust individual pieces without breaking anything apart.
👩‍💻 And right-clicking to pan in whiteboards, along with a new Back to content shortcut when you've zoomed too far out, makes navigating large boards significantly faster.
New looks to spark your next idea
Charts that inspire from the first click
Our chart library has had a glow up. You'll now find more realistic data examples, a refreshed colour palette with better contrast, and a fuller, more modern selection of chart types, so whatever you're building, you start from a great-looking baseline. Whether it's a report, a pitch, or a social post, the right chart is ready to go the moment you open it.
Publish and share anywhere
Share your work with a recognizable link
Every design you share now comes with the option to create a custom short link, so instead of a long, generic URL, you can set something clean and recognizable, like canva.link/my-brand-deck. It's a small detail that makes a real difference when you're sharing a portfolio, a pitch, or a campaign across email, social, or print.
Design it and sell it, without leaving Canva
The new PayPal app⁠(opens in a new tab or window) in Canva lets you embed payment links and QR codes directly into your designs, so anyone who sees your work can click or scan to complete a purchase through PayPal's checkout. Whether you're selling products, taking bookings, or running a promotion, you can go from design to done without needing a separate website or storefront.
Publish to more places, including your favorites

We've added new Publish apps to the share menu, so you can push designs directly to Facebook, Pinterest, OneDrive, Google Drive, Dropbox, and more. You can preview how your design will look on each platform before it goes live, set captions, cover images, and alt text, and publish with confidence that what you see is what your audience gets. Find them under ‘Share’, then ‘More ways to publish’.
Bring your HubSpot assets into Canva, and send designs straight back
The HubSpot app⁠(opens in a new tab or window) for Canva connects your marketing hub directly to your design workflow. Pull logos, product shots, and campaign imagery from HubSpot into Canva the moment you need them, create on-brand visuals, then publish finished designs back to HubSpot without downloading or re-uploading anything. For content teams managing multi-channel campaigns, product marketers building launch kits, and designers collaborating with campaign managers, it closes the loop between the tool you design in and the platform you market from.
Create product videos for Meta ads at scale
The Meta Catalog Data app⁠(opens in a new tab or window) lets you import your Meta product catalog directly into Canva, use it with Bulk Create to generate videos across your entire product range, then export them straight back to Meta, without manual work between steps. A template library of 16 vertical-specific templates covers the most common catalog categories, from eCommerce and retail to travel and automotive.
Design TikTok ads in Canva and go live in one step
The TikTok Ads app⁠(opens in a new tab or window) connects Canva directly to TikTok Ads Manager, so you can design using TikTok-optimised templates and publish your creative straight to a campaign without downloading or switching platforms. It joins LinkedIn Ads⁠(opens in a new tab or window) and Meta Ads⁠(opens in a new tab or window) as part of our growing suite of adtech apps , making Canva a single place to create and activate paid social content across the platforms that matter most.
Send your email designs straight from Canva
HTML email campaigns can now go from Canva straight to send. New integrations with Mailchimp⁠(opens in a new tab or window), Constant Contact⁠(opens in a new tab or window), Klaviyo⁠(opens in a new tab or window), and Flodesk⁠(opens in a new tab or window) connect your design workflow directly to your email platform, so there's no exporting, no rebuilding, and no gap between what you create and what lands in someone's inbox.

Vibe coding that matches your vision: Canva Code 2.0 is now available to all
Canva Code 2.0 is here: vibe code websites, apps and interactive experiences, then edit like a Canva design.
TLDR:
Vibe coding, the practice of using plain-language prompts to code, has quickly evolved from a tool for developers to new kind of creative medium that anyone can use to build apps, websites, games, and interactive experiences. But for many people, today’s tools can still feel technical and intimidating – and every output tends to look the same.
A decade ago, design required expensive subscriptions and an understanding of complex tools. Canva changed that with its simple and powerful drag-and-drop interface, and today, a quarter of a billion people use Canva every month to communicate their ideas visually. Now, we’re doing it again, but with code.
Starting today, Canva Code 2.0 is available to the entire Canva community. With new features that combine creative control with the latest models for AI-powered coding, we’re making it simple to design interactive experiences that are engaging, easy to build and customized to your brand.
Here’s what’s new in Canva Code:
Start from a prompt, a template or HTML
Every idea starts somewhere, and with Canva Code that starting point doesn’t have to be a blank page. You can now create with Canva Code right inside your other design projects, including as a page, in a whiteboard or deck. Get inspired with more than 50 new Canva Code templates for interactive designs, then personalize it with photos and graphics from our rich visual library or your own uploaded media.
If you’ve built something elsewhere, including other AI assistants, HTML import lets you bring that work into Canva as an editable design, so you can pick up where you left off without rebuilding from scratch.
Build and edit interactive experiences, all in one place
Canva Code combines the design power of Canva - easy editing of brand colors, texts or images, and a content library with over 120 million assets and over 50 templates - with outputs that work like websites or apps and can be published as an interactive experience.
Most vibe coding tools stop at functional, generating output that drowns in the sea of sameness. You might get a working prototype, but making it actually look like yours involves a complex editing surface, a separate design tool, a developer, or endless back-and-forth prompting that rarely lands where you want it.
Canva Code sits inside the same intuitive editor where you already house your brand kit. You can manually tweak your creation directly in the Canva Editor like any other design, or use Canva AI to prompt edits. It’s easy to swap in your own images by dragging directly from Canva's built-in library, update colors and fonts through the familiar toolbar, click into any section to retype text directly, or select a specific element to refine with conversational AI. The result is an interactive experience that works and looks like it came from you.

Create, collaborate and publish everywhere
The whole loop, from idea, to approval, to a website or app that your audience can engage with, happens in one place for everyone, including those who’ve never coded before. Teams can build, review and refine together in real time and comment right in the editor, turning vibe coding from a siloed pursuit into a team sport.
What you make together is then ready for wherever it needs to go next. Every Canva Code output is fully interactive and adopts automatically to any screen size, so you can preview how it will look on mobile. And when it’s time to publish, you can purchase a custom domain right inside Canva, publish to a free domain, or share securely within your organization using a single sign-on.
Unlocking creativity with code: What the Canva community is building
Early adopters of Canva Code have proven that code is more than a technical tool – it’s a new medium for education, marketing, entrepreneurship, staying organized and so much more.
Since we first introduced Canva Code a year ago, our community has coded more than six million sites, with creations spanning from classroom hubs to real estate listings and team ice breakers. That momentum reflects a shift we hear from our community: people don’t just want static content, they want to build experiences that feel polished, useful, and unmistakably theirs.
Small businesses, like Alt Marketing School, are building mini apps to provide fundraising training and planning for their communities: an app to brainstorm fundraising leads through content and a system to score potential fundraising channels. Alt Marketing School also created an interactive roadmap on what’s coming up for its members.
Educators and school administrators are using Canva Code to enhance the learning and social environment. One teacher built bespoke webpages for each of their classrooms to keep students and parents updated on all announcements. Another teacher created a form, published it as a website, and connected to Canva sheets for data to use for potlucks, events, or track top books read for prizes.
For World Book Day, 50 passionate readers created educational games across different subjects with Canva Code and a pedagogical description of how to use the games in the learning environment.
Empowering everyone to experience the future of design
We believe tools should never put a limit on your imagination, and AI has transformed the creative process on Canva, with over 32 billion uses of our AI products to date. Whether through code, design, writing, image generation or beyond, it’s accelerating how we empower the world to design anything, in a workflow that’s as simple as possible.
For the more than 265 million people who turn to Canva each month to design their goals, this unlocks another way to achieve their goals. Canva Code reflects the evolution of design from presentations and social posts to now including visual websites, web apps and interactive experiences. No matter what you’re creating, it should always look and feel like yours. Canva Code 2.0 is now available to free, pro, business, enterprise, and education users.

Canva hosted 60+ interns in a single recent cohort, all working on a product used by 260 million monthly active users, and it fills those seats in a 30-day window. For the 2027–2028 cycle, the ANZ summer program (December 2027 start) is expected to open applications around April 2027, while US summer roles (May–August 2028) typically post September through November. That 30-day ANZ window isn't a suggestion: Prosple’s listing documented a late-April open and late-May close for the last cycle, and Reddit users report that positions close when filled, not when the calendar says so.
What Is a Canva Internship?
A Canva internship is a paid, 12-week summer placement that puts penultimate-year students into real product teams at one of the world’s largest private tech companies, valued at $42–65 billion. Interns ship features used by 260 million monthly active users across design, engineering, data, and marketing tracks. The program starts with a one-week onboarding bootcamp and is remote-friendly: "if you want to do work from the office, at home, or a bit of both, it’s completely up to you." Glassdoor rates Canva 3.9 out of 5 from 862 reviews, with intern interviews scoring a 67% positive experience rate. The 37 former interns who transitioned to full-time through Canva’s Launchpad program show the pipeline is real.
When Do Canva Internship Applications Open for 2027–2028?
Canva’s calendar splits across two hemispheres, and the distinction matters more than most applicants realize. The ANZ summer program (December start) opens applications around April, keeps the window live for roughly 30 days, and closes by late May. The US summer program (May–August) posts roles September through November on a rolling basis. For the 2027–2028 cycle, that means the ANZ window is expected around April–May 2027 (about 8 months before the December start), while US roles should appear September–November 2027. The overall interview process runs 4–5 weeks from recruiter call to decision, which is fast by tech standards. One thing to note: Canva has not posted 2027–2028 dates yet, so registering interest via their Early Careers page is the only way to catch the window when it opens.

Why You Must Apply the Week Applications Open
Canva’s official Early Careers page says the internship is a 12-week program for penultimate-year students, and Prosple’s listing documented that "roles will be live for 30 days." Thirty days is the entire window, and review is rolling inside it. Reddit confirms the pattern: one thread notes that applications were still being accepted in mid-May for a recent intake, with the board closing shortly after. Another thread asks if anyone even got the OA, and the answer was mostly rejections. The math is simple: a 30-day window with rolling review means late applicants compete for whatever seats the first two weeks didn’t fill.

Which Canva Internship Programs Should You Target?
Seven confirmed internship tracks span engineering, design, data, and business. Which one should you pick? The honest answer is the one whose skills you can already show, because each track interviews against its own technical bar. And one common thread runs through all of them: product thinking, the ability to connect your work to outcomes for 260 million users.
| Program | Focus | Duration | Key skills |

| ML / AI Engineering | AI design suggestions, image generation, text effects, content recommendation | 12 weeks | Python, PyTorch, deep learning, model deployment, math/stats |
| Product Design | Editor features, templates, enterprise products | 12 weeks | Visual design, product thinking, UX research, portfolio required |

See all open roles at lifeatcanva.com/en/jobs. And note the split calendar: ANZ roles recruit about 8 months ahead for a December start, while US roles recruit September–November for a May–August start. Canva also runs the separate Launchpad program for recent graduates, a 12-month full-time track that many interns convert into.
What Are the Eligibility Requirements?
Canva publishes the same core requirements across its internship tracks:
• Enrollment: penultimate-year (second-to-last year) tertiary student. Canva’s official early careers page says the program is for "penultimate year tertiary students," and FinalRoundAI reports expected graduation dates of Dec 2026 to Jun 2028 for the current cycle.
• Degree fields: CS, Design, Statistics, or closely related disciplines for engineering and design tracks. Marketing and other tracks have their own requirements.
• Work authorization: Australian work rights required for Sydney and Melbourne roles. US work authorization preferred for Austin and San Francisco. No explicit visa sponsorship language found in any posting.
• Availability: the full 12 weeks. The program is remote-friendly: "if you want to do work from the office, at home, or a bit of both, it’s completely up to you."
Does Canva Have a GPA Cutoff?
No. No GPA requirement appears in any Canva internship posting, FAQ, or careers page. This is verified absence, not omission: Canva’s official how-we-hire page emphasizes skills and product thinking over academic scores, and explicitly says "even if you don’t think you quite meet all of the skills listed or tick all the boxes, we’d still love to hear from you." What actually gates you? Two things. The penultimate-year requirement excludes graduating seniors and first-year students alike. And work-authorization requirements vary by office: Australian work rights for Sydney/Melbourne, US authorization for Austin/SF. Beyond that, Canva screens for product-building experience, technical skills, and alignment with its "Crazy Big Goals" culture.

What Skills Does Canva Look For, and How Do You Build Them?
Across seven confirmed internship tracks, Canva’s job descriptions and interview reports reveal a consistent hierarchy. AI literacy shows up in every single track: Canva’s official stance is "we encourage you to use AI at every stage of the hiring process" and they "judge you on how you use AI." Product thinking is the other universal: the ability to connect technical work to outcomes for 260 million users. Below that, the technical asks split by track: Python spans four of seven, Java matters specifically for the backend OA, and design craft matters for two. What does that pattern tell you? Canva hires people who can build with AI and think in products, then trains the vertical.

What Is the Canva Application and Interview Process Like?
Canva’s funnel is structured and runs about 4–5 weeks from recruiter call to decision:
1. Apply at lifeatcanva.com with your resume. You’ll get a confirmation email immediately. About 1–2 weeks later, a recruiter reviews your application and, if successful, arranges a Zoom call.
2. Recruiter Zoom call (20–30 min). Aspirations, experience, and culture fit. Canva calls this the "initial conversation" and says it kicks off the 4–5 week process.
3. Online Assessment (90 min, 3 questions). For backend SWE, this is Java-only with no other language options. ML/AI adds math/stats-heavy MCQs. Reddit consensus: "Hardest part of Canva’s intern process is passing the OA."
4. Technical interview and offer. SWE: LeetCode easy/easy-medium plus system design. ML/AI: 75-minute final (15 min behavioral + 60 min technical coding, AI-assisted). Offers specify team, location, and compensation.
One thing that makes Canva’s process unusual: they explicitly encourage AI use at every stage, including interviews. "Just be ready to explain how you used it, what you kept, changed, or built on." The behavioral portion uses the STARR method (Situation, Task, Action, Results, Reflection), not standard STAR, so practice adding the Reflection step. Glassdoor rates intern interview difficulty 3 out of 5 with an average 22-day process.

How Do You Stand Out When 60 Seats Fill in 30 Days?
Three moves, all executable before April. First, apply in week one of the window. Rolling review plus positions that close when filled makes timing itself a filter. Second, build the evidence Canva actually evaluates: product-thinking projects, AI-assisted development workflow, and portfolio proof that you shipped something. Canva’s interviewers use the STARR method and explicitly ask how you use AI tools, so having a project where you used AI to build, tested the output, and iterated on it's worth more than another LeetCode solve. Third, prepare for the OA like it’s the real gate, because Reddit says it's. For backend, that means Java fluency (no language choice). For ML, it means brushing up on math and stats fundamentals alongside coding. The technical interview after the OA is reportedly easier. And remember what 37 Launchpad conversions tell you: the internship is a 12-week audition for a full-time role.

FAQ
When do Canva internship applications open for 2027–2028?
For the ANZ summer program (December 2027 start), applications typically open in April and stay live for about 30 days, closing in late May. For US summer roles (May–August 2028), postings appear September through November. Canva has not posted 2027–2028 dates yet, so register your interest at lifeatcanva.com/en/early-careers/ and check back early 2027.
Is Canva internship recruiting rolling?
Partially. The ANZ intake has a defined 30-day application window (typically April–May), while US roles reportedly recruit on a rolling basis from September. In both cases, positions close when filled, so applying early within the window gives you the best chance. Reddit users report high rejection rates even at the OA stage.
What GPA or grades do you need for a Canva internship?
Canva doesn't publish a minimum GPA requirement. Their official hiring page emphasizes skills, product thinking, and cultural alignment over academic scores. They explicitly encourage candidates to apply even if they don’t tick all the boxes. Focus on demonstrating product-building experience, technical skills, and alignment with Canva’s Crazy Big Goals culture.
What is the Canva interview process like?
For engineering interns, expect a 90-minute online assessment (3 coding questions, Java-only for backend), followed by a recruiter Zoom call, then a technical interview with LeetCode-style problems and system design. ML/AI adds math-heavy MCQs. The process takes about 4–5 weeks. Canva encourages using AI tools and asks you to explain how you used them.
Do Canva interns get return offers?
Return-offer rates vary significantly by year and market conditions. Third-party estimates put the normal rate around 60%, but during hiring freezes (like 2024–2025), the rate dropped as low as 11% with almost no external grad roles. Canva’s Launchpad program is the primary pipeline from internship to full-time. 37 former interns returned through Launchpad in one cohort.
What skills does Canva look for in interns?
Canva values product thinking across all tracks, the ability to connect technical work to user outcomes for 260 million monthly users. Engineers need Python or Java plus framework experience. ML roles need deep learning and PyTorch. Designers need a portfolio showing product and visual craft. All tracks are evaluated on AI literacy: how you use AI tools, what you kept, changed, or built on.
Are Canva internships paid?
Yes. Australian SWE interns earn approximately A$28–38 per hour (A$61K–79K annualized) with meals provided. US roles reportedly pay $46–60 per hour for SWE, with ML/AI trending higher at $52–60 per hour. US interns receive relocation assistance for Austin and San Francisco. Canva pays 18% above the Australian national average for SWE interns.
Is the Canva backend OA really Java-only?
Yes. Multiple Reddit reports confirm the backend SWE online assessment is Java-only with no other language options. This is a major differentiator versus most tech companies that allow language choice. The OA is 90 minutes for 3 questions at roughly medium difficulty. ML/AI OAs are different: math and stats heavy with both MCQs and coding, and language choice may vary.
The window is 30 days long and the review inside it's rolling. Spend the runway building proof: a remote Externship turns "interested in tech" into a finished AI or product project an April application can point at.

What is a balance sheet?
A balance sheet is a document that shows the financial health of a company at a specific point in time, usually at the end of every quarter or year. It lists all the business’s assets (resources owned) and liabilities (obligations owed) to determine the net assets or equity. Its name comes from its need to be “balanced,” meaning the total assets should equal the sum of the business’s liabilities and equity.
It's also called a statement of financial position, as it provides a snapshot of the company’s financial situation within a given reporting date, rather than its financial activities over time.
The balance sheet serves two purposes, depending on the person viewing the report. When viewed internally, it helps stakeholders gain clarity on whether the business is succeeding or not. It allows them to make necessary adjustments or focus on the positives. When viewed externally, it provides potential investors with insight into the business’s resources and its financial structure.
As a financial report, balance sheets are used across different industries and fields to aid decision-making and assess the overall financial health of an organization. It's not just limited to businesses, as personal balance sheet templates are a popular way to determine a person’s net worth.
For an easy-to-use balance sheet template, try Canva Sheets⁠(opens in a new tab or window). Create a custom financial report by entering the details of your assets and liabilities to calculate your equity.

Key components of a balance sheet
The balance sheet primarily focuses on this core equation:
assets = liabilities + equity
Based on this formula, a typical balance sheet format has three key components:
Assets
This is defined as anything a business or entity owns that holds value and can be converted to cash. It’s recorded as a positive (+) in a simple balance sheet template. An asset is further categorized into current and noncurrent assets.
Current assets are anything that a business expects to be converted into cash within a year. These can be cash and other cash equivalents, inventory, prepaid expenses, accounts receivable, and marketable securities.
Noncurrent assets are long-term investments that aren’t easily convertible to cash quickly, such as land, brands, trademarks, intellectual property, and equipment.
Liabilities
A liability is anything that a business owes to a third-party entity. It can be financial or legal obligations and is recorded as a negative (-) in a balance sheet template. A liability can also include an obligation to provide goods and services in the future. It's also further categorized as a current liability or a noncurrent liability.
A current liability includes anything due within a year. This can be payroll, rent, utilities, accounts payable, debt financing, and other accrued expenses.
Noncurrent liabilities are the long-term obligations that are not due within a year. These can be leases, bonds payable, loans, deferred tax liabilities, and provisions for pensions.
Equity
This is the last of the balance sheet elements. It’s also called owner’s equity or shareholders’ equity. It refers to the value remaining for owners after all the liabilities are accounted for. Equity typically consists of contributed capital and retained earnings.

Balance sheet FAQs
Why is a balance sheet important?
A balance sheet is important because it provides an essential snapshot of a business’s financial situation—assets, liabilities, and equity. This is crucial for assessing the overall financial health, liquidity, and solvency. The balance sheet is also a primary document for making informed financial decisions.
How to read a balance sheet?
Reading a balance sheet requires understanding its structure and the key balance sheet elements. You need to confirm its report date and that its fundamental equation holds in the report. It might also be necessary to assess the financial health by evaluating key balance sheet ratios and comparing the current report with previous ones.
What is the difference between a balance sheet and an income statement?
Although they're both key financial statements, the difference between a balance sheet and an income statement lies in their purpose. A balance sheet shows the financial position at a specific point in time. This tells you what the business owns and owes as of that specific date. Meanwhile, an income statement shows the business’s financial performance over a certain period. This tells you how much money the business has made or lost over a specified duration.

Kelly Steckelberg named as Canva's new CFO
 Make us a preferred source Make us a preferred source on Google
Link copied Copy failed
The news: Australian technology company Canva has appointed Kelly Steckelberg, former Zoom chief financial officer, as its new CFO. Steckelberg joins the company as it reaches a new valuation of $US32 billion ($48.8 billion) and reports significant user growth.
The numbers: In an announcement, Canva said it has reached $2.5 billion in annualised revenue and increased its monthly active users to 220 million, up from 200 million in the previous month. The company has maintained profitability for seven consecutive years and added 1,000 new employees in 2024. Its enterprise offering is now used by more than 95% of Fortune 500 companies.
The context: The CFO appointment comes as Canva continues its expansion into enterprise markets, with the company reporting a tripling of enterprise revenue growth in the past year. Notable enterprise clients include HP, Snowflake and Docusign.
The company has also launched new artificial intelligence products including Dream Lab, powered by Leonardo.Ai, and Magic Studio, which was recognised in TIME's Best Inventions list.
Former chief financial officer Damien Singh resigned from the design software startup earlier this year after the company launched an internal investigation amid concerns about alleged inappropriate behaviour.
What they said: "Kelly's impressive track record as a strong leader and strategic thinker, combined with her proven expertise in scaling enterprise companies, makes her the perfect addition to our leadership bench," said Cliff Obrecht, Canva co-founder and chief operating officer.
"I've been an admirer of the team, product and mission for a number of years now and I'm eager to have the opportunity to work alongside Melanie, Cliff, Cameron and the team to continue empowering every person and organisation to achieve their goals," Steckelberg said.
The source: Canva Press Release

Canva, a high-valued design software startup that competes with Adobe, said Monday that it hired Kelly Steckelberg as its chief financial officer, five years after she helped take Zoom public and then guided the company through its Covid-19 pandemic surge.
Founded in 2013, Canva was valued recently at $32 billion, a drop from its peak of $40 billion in 2021.
"Kelly's impressive track record as a strong leader and strategic thinker, combined with her proven expertise in scaling enterprise companies, make her the perfect addition to our leadership bench," Canva said in an emailed statement.
Canva is generating about $2.5 billion in annualized revenue and boasts 220 million monthly users. The company is widely viewed as a top initial public offering candidate for venture-backed tech companies after a historically slow period for new offerings dating back to early 2022.
On Monday, ServiceTitan, which sells software for the trades, filed to list on the Nasdaq. Cerebras, a maker of artificial intelligence chips, has been on file since late September, and online lender Klarna said last week that it has confidentially filed its IPO paperwork with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission.
A Canva spokesperson declined to comment on the startup's timeline for an IPO.
Steckelberg held financial positions at Cisco and was CEO of online dating company Zoosk before joining Zoom in 2017. Steckelberg is based in Austin, Texas, while Canva has its headquarters in Sydney, Australia.
Zoom went public with Steckelberg's help in 2019. The video-chat company saw its market cap soar to upward of $160 billion in October 2020, early in the Covid-19 pandemic, as users working from home swarmed to the app. Zoom has since lost more than 85% of its value.
Steckelberg announced her departure from Zoom in August after seven years at the company. Last month, former Microsoft executive Michelle Chang replaced Steckelberg as Zoom's CFO.
Canva's previous finance chief Damien Singh resigned in February after the company said it was conducting an internal investigation surrounding inappropriate behavior.

Canva smacked with $792,000 in fines for lodging FY24 financials 11 months late
Canva hit with $792K in ASIC fines for late financials—discover how a tech unicorn handles profit talk versus billion-dollar losses.
Simon Thomsen   Simon Thomsen
Icon
Share

Prefer Startup Daily
Canva rap 
The Canva rap at 2024's Canva Create launch.
Corporate cop the Australian Securities and Investment Commission (ASIC) has issued four infringement notices worth $198,000 each – $792,000 in total – to four companies in the Australian Canva Group for failing to lodge financial reports on time.
The business got off lightly in a broader ASIC crackdown on late lodgements, which has also seen cosmetics group Mecca, Bing Lee, drink bottle maker Frank Green and burger chain Grill’d among those also handed penalty notices.
Canva only filed its 2021 and 2022 annual financial statements last September, and the 2023 and 2024 accounts on March 27 this year. The 2025 accounts were filed on time last week.
Canva’s former long-term chief financial officer Damien Singh, left the business suddenly in early 2024, and was replaced by Texas-based Kelly Steckelberg 10 months later.
The fines were handed to Canva Pty Ltd, Canva Operations Pty Ltd, Canva Trading Pty Ltd, and Fusion Books Pty Ltd for the 2024 financial reports and not lodging them by the 30 April, 2025 deadline.
Unlike when you pay a speeding fine, paying an ASIC infringement notice is not an admission of guilt or liability, and the companies fined are not regarded as having been convicted of the alleged offence. The $198,000 penalty is half the $396,000 maximum if the matter goes to court.

The four Canva businesses restructured into a single entity, Canva Australia Holdings Pty Ltd, last year.
No late note
When asked by Startup Daily to explain why they were so late, the company declined to comment.
Instead a Canva spokesperson was keen to emphasise that the company was profitable “on a free cash flow basis” for the past nine years.
“We continue to generate significantly more cash than we use, with operating cash flow nearly doubling in 2024 while building strong and growing cash reserves,” the spokesperson said.
But the financials lodged with ASIC paid a different picture, with nearly $1 billion of statutory losses posted over three years between 2022 and 2024.
Revenue more than doubled in that period, rising from US$962m in 2022 to US$1.44bn the following year and $US2.1bn in 2024. Expenses rose by US$600m in 12 months to US$2.3bn in 2024. The combined financial losses totalled US$692m (A$955m), including a US$242m (A$335m) loss in 2024.
Cash flow v losses
The financial reports said operating cash flow increased from US$133m in 2023 to US$263m in 2024. By the end of the year, the company had nearly A$1 billion in cash reserves – no doubt handy for cofounder Cliff Obrecht’s acquisition ambitions.
“Our reported results for this period include non-cash expenses from shares in Canva given to our team, rather than cash leaving the business,” the Canva spokesperson said.
“This can impact how our results are interpreted and does not reflect the underlying strength of our performance.”
Canva is was valued at US$42bn (A$58bn) in mid 2025 following secondary share sales.
Perhaps more of those cash reserves could have been invested in financial auditors, sooner.
ASIC Commissioner Kate O’Rourke was more interested in deadlines than free cash flow.
“ASIC is undertaking targeted, data-driven surveillance to identify non‑lodgement and persistent late lodgement of financial reports,” she said.
‘Companies and other entities with reporting obligations must ensure financial reports are lodged within the required timeframes. Both non-lodgement and late lodgement prevents creditors and other users of the reports from making timely and informed decisions when dealing with these companies and is a failure of their legal obligations.”
All up, ASIC has issued, and received payment for 21 infringement notices worth more than $4 million for alleged FY24 financial reporting breaches.
